1. Aim

To determine the wavelength of light emitted by a mercury vapour lamp using a plane transmission diffraction grating and a spectrometer.

What you will learn

  • How a grating produces multiple orders of the spectrum.
  • How the diffraction angle θn depends on the order n and wavelength λ.
  • How to eliminate errors by taking readings on both sides of the direct image (and on both verniers).
  • How a graph of sin θ vs order n gives a straight line whose slope yields λ.

2.1 Experimental setup — Optical Spectrometer (top view)

Fig. 3b — Optical Spectrometer (source: WCTM Gurgaon, Physics-I Lab Manual, Fig. 2). The collimator delivers a parallel beam, the grating is mounted on the prism table at 45° to the incident beam, and the telescope is positioned 45° on the other side to receive the first-order diffracted image.

3. Theory

Diffraction is the spreading of light waves into the geometrical shadow region when they pass through narrow apertures or around obstacles, especially when the size of the obstacle/aperture is comparable to the wavelength of light.

3.1 The Plane Diffraction Grating

A plane diffraction grating is an optically flat glass plate on which a large number of equidistant, parallel straight lines have been ruled. The ruled lines act as opaque regions and the space between any two adjacent lines is transparent.

If a = width of one transparent slit and b = width of one opaque line, then:

Grating element (a + b) = 2.54 / N (in cm, when N is lines/inch)

Points separated by distance (a+b) are called corresponding points.

Fig. 3a — Diffraction of light through a plane diffraction grating (source: BrainKart, 12th Physics — Wave Optics, Fig. 6.66).

3.2 Condition for Primary Maxima

When a parallel beam of monochromatic light is incident normally on the grating, the condition for the nth order principal maximum is:

(a + b) sin θn = n λ    — (1)

where n is the order (0, 1, 2, 3 …) and λ is the wavelength of the light used.

For 1st order (n = 1):

(a + b) sin θ1 = λ    — (2)

3.3 Graphical Method (most accurate)

Equation (1) can be re-written as

sin θn = ( λ / (a+b) ) × n

A plot of sin θn (y-axis) versus order n (x-axis) is a straight line through the origin with slope = λ / (a+b). Therefore

λ = slope × (a + b)

Using two or more orders averages out random errors and is preferred over the single-order formula.

4. Procedure

1
Initial adjustments. Focus the eye-piece of the telescope so the cross-wires are sharp. Focus the telescope on a distant object for parallel rays. Level the spectrometer using the levelling screws and the prism table using the spirit level.
2
Mount the grating. Fix the grating stand on the prism table (two screws in the holes along a line parallel to screws P–Q). The clamp face should be at the centre. Hold the grating by its edge only and clamp it with the ruled surface facing the telescope.
3
Optical levelling of the grating. Tilt the table to about 45° and rotate the telescope to receive the slit image reflected from the grating. Make this image symmetric about the horizontal cross-wire using screw R — the grating plane is now vertical. Rotate the table so the grating is perpendicular to the collimator; bring the vertical cross-wire on the 1st-order image and centre it with screws P or Q. Repeat on the other side — the image should be symmetric in all positions.
4
Grating normal to the incident light. Align the telescope with the collimator and note the reading; add 90° and place the telescope there (perpendicular to the collimator). Rotate the grating table so the grating face is normal to the collimator — turn the table to make the slit image fall on the vertical cross-wire, then rotate by 45° to set the grating normal to the incident light (ruled side away from the collimator). Clamp the table.
5
Locate the 1st-order spectrum. Look from in front of the collimator; as you move toward the telescope you'll see the 1st-order diffracted image. Bring the telescope onto it, clamp it, and use the fine screw to align the vertical cross-wire on the slit centre. Note the reading on both verniers (V1 & V2). Repeat on the other side of the direct image.
6
2nd-order spectrum. Move the telescope further out and take readings for the 2nd-order diffracted image, again on both sides of the direct image and on both verniers.
7
Repeat the entire observation set three times for consistency.
8
Note N (lines/inch) marked on the grating, and store the grating carefully with the ruled side up.

8. Viva-Voce & Short Questions (for exam prep)

Q1. What is a diffraction grating?
A plane diffraction grating is an optically flat glass plate on which a large number of equidistant parallel lines are ruled. The ruled parts are opaque, the spaces are transparent, and the sum (a+b) of one transparent + one opaque width is the grating element.
Q2. State the condition for principal maxima in a grating.
(a + b) sin θn = n λ , where n is the order, θn is the diffraction angle, λ the wavelength, and (a+b) the grating element.
Q3. Why are readings taken on both sides of the direct image?
To eliminate the error due to non-coincidence of the rotation axis of the telescope with the axis of the grating table (i.e. the zero-error of the spectrometer).
Q4. Why are two verniers used?
To remove the error due to the centre of the graduated circle not being concentric with the axis of rotation. The mean of V1 and V2 gives a more accurate reading.
Q5. What is the resolving power of a grating?
R = λ/Δλ = nN, where n is the order of the spectrum and N is the total number of lines illuminated on the grating.
Q6. Why is the yellow line of mercury (5770 Å) not resolved into a doublet in 1st order in ordinary lab gratings?
The doublet separation is only 6 Å. Resolving power nN in 1st order is too small (R ≈ 12,500 for N = 12,500 lines) to separate 6 Å at 5770 Å, so it appears as one line.
Q7. What would happen if the grating is not normal to the incident light?
The path difference changes, the formula becomes (a+b)(sin i ± sin θ) = nλ, and both the angle of incidence i and diffraction θ enter — leading to a more complicated (and erroneous) result.
Q8. What is the role of the collimator?
It produces a parallel beam of light from the slit so that the condition for diffraction (parallel incident beam) is satisfied.
Q9. Why do we prefer the graphical method?
It uses data from multiple orders, so random errors are averaged out. It also gives a visible check — the best-fit line should pass through the origin; any deviation indicates a systematic error.
Q10. How is the wavelength of an unknown source determined with a grating?
Repeat the experiment with the unknown source. The grating element (a+b) and the order n are kept the same. From the measured diffraction angle θ, use (a+b) sin θ = n λ to compute λ.

9. Precautions

  1. Always hold the grating by its edges; never touch the ruled surface.
  2. Adjust the telescope and collimator for parallel rays before mounting the grating.
  3. The grating must be exactly normal to the incident light from the collimator.
  4. The slit should be narrow and vertical for sharp spectral lines.
  5. Take readings on both sides of the direct image and on both verniers.
  6. Repeat each set of readings at least three times for consistency.
  7. Do not move the spectrometer or grating once the experiment has started.
  8. Do not look at the mercury lamp directly — use the spectrometer eye-piece.
